source: Koriat (2012) The self-consistency model of subjective confidence. Psychological Review 119(1):80-113
finding: Confidence is the consistency with which a chosen answer is supported across a sample of retrieved representations. It works like a statistical level of confidence: the chance that a new sample gives the same choice. The confidence-accuracy link is a by-product of a consistency-correctness link. It is positive when consistently chosen answers are usually right, and negative when wrong answers are favoured. Overconfidence comes from confidence tracking reliability while calibration is scored against correctness. Response speed is a cheap cue for consistency. Accessibility (amount that comes to mind) adds an independent contribution.
numbers: Abstract only. No effect sizes or N obtained: the paper is paywalled. The abstract says the predicted pattern was confirmed for several different tasks.
quote: confidence on the consistency with which the chosen answer is supported across representations
limits: Abstract read on PubMed, not the full paper. Human two-alternative tasks. Per-task N and r sit in the paper and were not obtained.
agent_relevance: This is the human version of confidence from agreement among samples. It predicts the failure we must guard against: where the modal answer is wrong, confidence is high and wrong.

source: Koriat (2008) Subjective confidence in one's answers: the consensuality principle. JEP:LMC 34(4):945-959
finding: Within-person confidence-accuracy correlation is positive for items whose consensual answer is correct and negative for items whose consensual answer is wrong. Consensual answers are reached faster and chosen more consistently by the same person on different occasions. This argues against direct access to correctness. Confidence is accurate only while responses are mostly correct across the sampled items.
numbers: Abstract only; no N or r obtained.
limits: Abstract read. General-information questions only. Consensually wrong items are picked on purpose, so the negative correlation is a design result, not the natural mix.
agent_relevance: Gives the human precedent for a consensually wrong test set. Build such a set for the agent (items where the sampled majority is wrong) and report the sign of the agreement-accuracy relation on it.

source: Koriat (2011) Subjective confidence in perceptual judgments: a test of the self-consistency model. JEP:General 140(1):117-139
finding: Predictions of the self-consistency model, first confirmed for general knowledge and social attitudes, also held for perceptual judgments. Confidence correlated with how consensual the choice was, not with whether it was correct. This is a replication in a new domain by the same lab.
numbers: Abstract only; no numbers obtained.
limits: Same author and lab as the original. Other labs' replications are in d05.
agent_relevance: Domain-general support: the agreement-to-confidence link is not specific to memory questions.

source: Koriat (1976) Another look at the relationship between phonetic symbolism and the feeling of knowing. Memory & Cognition 4(3):244-248
finding: Early finding of the consensus effect. For items with a consensually correct response, accuracy rose with confidence. For items with a consensually incorrect response, accuracy fell with confidence. Consensual responses felt more compelling whatever their correctness.
numbers: Abstract only; no numbers obtained.
limits: Old study; word-matching task. Cited only to date the idea.
agent_relevance: The confidently wrong consensus pattern is 50 years old and appeared in the first test. A confidence signal built on agreement inherits it by design.

source: Koriat (2025, epub 2024) Subjective confidence as a monitor of the replicability of the response. Perspect Psychol Sci 20(4):744-761
finding: Full text read. Items were split into consensually correct (CC, more right than wrong answers) and consensually wrong (CW). CC items give the usual positive confidence-accuracy correlation. CW items give a negative one: people were more confident in wrong answers than right ones, and for each item those choosing the wrong answer were more confident. This held for 16 different tasks. Other labs found the same: Brewer and colleagues (deceptive vs non-deceptive sentences), face recognition (Sampaio 2017), syllogisms (Bajsanski 2019), mammogram diagnosis (Litvinova 2022). Koriat now argues confidence tracks replicability (how likely the same choice is to recur). In 10 studies the confidence-replicability correlation was significant within and between individuals, for both CC and CW items. Partialling out replicability accounted for both the positive and negative confidence-accuracy correlations.
numbers: 16 tasks show the CC positive / CW negative pattern; 10 studies for the replicability test. Exact r and N sit in supplementary tables S2-S6, which were not read.
limits: Author's own synthesis, so study selection is his. CW items were built in on purpose; he says the positive correlation holds in the natural mix. No failed replication appears in this text, but the author did not look for one.
agent_relevance: Strongest available human evidence for gap 3: consistency-based confidence works in the natural mix and flips sign on consensually wrong items. Seen by at least four other groups. For the agent: expect agreement to be a good signal on most items and an inverted one on a small set of systematic-error items.

source: Koriat (2015) When two heads are better than one and when they can be worse: the amplification hypothesis. JEP:General 144(5):934-950
finding: Picking the more confident member of a pair (maximum confidence slating) beat the better member on consensually correct items but was worse than the worse member on consensually wrong items. Group discussion amplified this further. On CW items interaction lowered accuracy and raised confidence in the wrong answers.
numbers: Abstract only; perceptual and general-information tasks; no numbers obtained.
limits: Abstract read only. Human pairs.
agent_relevance: Direct warning for confidence-weighted voting over samples or agents: weighting by confidence amplifies whatever the majority tendency is, good or bad. Test any CISC-style weighting on a consensually wrong slice, not only on the average.

source: Farquhar, Kossen, Kuhn, Gal (2024) Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy. Nature
finding: Full open-access text read. Semantic entropy clusters sampled answers by meaning (bidirectional entailment judged by GPT-3.5 in the default) and takes entropy over the clusters. Averaged over 30 model-task combinations, AUROC was 0.790 for semantic entropy against 0.691 naive entropy, 0.698 P(True) and 0.687 embedding regression. It stayed at 0.78-0.81 across LLaMA, Falcon, Mistral and 7B-70B. Ten generations were used. For GPT-4 (no probabilities exposed then) a discrete variant was used on paragraph-length biographies: split the text into factual claims, rebuild a question for each, draw 3 new answers per question plus the original claim. This beat a self-check and a paragraph P(True) on AUROC and AURAC, though P(True) had a narrow edge once the 20% most doubtful answers were rejected.
numbers: 30 model-task combinations (sentence-length answers 96 +/- 70 characters); AUROC 0.790 vs 0.691 / 0.698 / 0.687; 10 generations; FactualBio has 21 people and 150 claims, GPT-4.
quote: it does not guarantee factuality because it does not help when LLM outputs are systematically bad
limits: The authors state the method does not address systematic errors: models consistently wrong from common misconceptions, reward hacking or systematic reasoning failure. Entailment clustering costs extra model calls. 2023-era models; no frontier reasoning model. The paragraph-level AUROC value itself was only in a figure.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 9. Also an authoritative admission for gap 2: agreement-based uncertainty fails on consistent wrong answers. For code, replace entailment with test execution as the equivalence check.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs (CISC): cost of the self-check
finding: Re-read for gap 6. The P(True)-style self-check is appended to the same generated prefix as one extra prompt of about 20 tokens plus one generated token, so the prefix is not reprocessed. The paper calls the overhead negligible next to a sample of hundreds of tokens. The 46% saving counts samples only: self-consistency needed 18.6 samples on average to match CISC with 10. Verbalized 1-100 gave 30% and token response probability 31% at budget 10.
numbers: Table 1 (macro-average over models and datasets), P(True): 41% (8.4 samples) at budget 5 and 46% (18.6) at budget 10; accuracy gain 1.6% and 1.1%. Verbal 1-100: 22% and 30%. Models: Gemma2, Qwen2.5 (7 models), Mistral 8B/22B/123B. Datasets GSM8K, MATH, MMLU, BBH.
limits: Open models up to 123B, none a reasoning model. The overhead claim assumes the prefix is cached. On an API that bills input tokens again, the extra call re-bills the whole prefix (my reading, not tested in the paper). Softmax temperature was tuned per method.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 mostly closed for self-hosted or cached-prefix serving: the self-check costs about 20 input tokens and 1 output token, so the saving survives. Without prefix caching the cost is roughly the input price of each sample again; recompute before adopting. Open: whether a reasoning model can still rank its own samples (WQD 52-62% here).

source: Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Full text read. Token confidence is the mean negative log-probability of the top-k tokens. Trace quality is scored from sliding groups of tokens (window 2,048): lowest group, bottom-10% groups, or the last 2,048 tokens. Online, a trace is cut when its current group confidence falls below a threshold set from 16 warm-up traces, and sampling stops at 95% consensus. The 84.7% token saving is the best single cell (DeepConf-low). Across models and sets DeepConf-low saves about 43.8% to 84.7% and DeepConf-high 18.8% to 59.0%.
numbers: Offline, 512 traces: DeepSeek-8B AIME25 82.3 -> 87.4 (tail confidence, keep top 10%); Qwen3-32B AIME24 85.3 -> 90.8 (bottom-10%, keep top 10%); GPT-OSS-120B AIME25 97.0 -> 99.9. Online DeepSeek-8B mean token saving 62.88% (low) and 47.67% (high). Accuracy fell in a few cells, e.g. Qwen3-32B BRUMO25 -0.9 points; the authors note 10% filtering can hurt through overconfident wrong traces, as with GPT-OSS-120B.
limits: Needs token log-probabilities and control of generation, so it runs on open-weights serving, not on a plain chat API. The authors name overconfident wrong traces as the main limitation. Math and GPQA-D only. Savings are against full 512-trace voting, a very large baseline.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: the headline holds only with logprobs and a huge trace budget. For a closed API we can copy the consensus-stop part (d10) but not the token filter. Agreement among partial traces as a replacement is untested here.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: Agreement among the samples drawn so far decides when to stop. A Dirichlet model gives the chance that the current leader stays the leader; stop when it passes a threshold. It needs only the sampled answers, no logprobs, so it works with any API.
numbers: 17 reasoning and code datasets, 3 LLMs. Sample budget cut by up to 7.9x; average 3.3x with a 0.04% accuracy drop over reasoning categories. By model: GPT-3.5-turbo 4.4x with under 0.2% drop, Code-davinci-002 3.4x, Vicuna-13B 1.9x. At equal average sample cost it beat plain self-consistency by up to 5 points.
limits: 2023 models. Stops on completed samples, not partial traces. Saves cost only; it does not make the confidence rank right and wrong better. Code tasks need an answer-equivalence key such as test outputs.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partial answer: an agreement-only, logprob-free stop rule exists and saves 2-8x samples at near-zero accuracy cost on older models. Agreement among partial (unfinished) traces is still untested.

source: Kang et al. (2025) Scalable Best-of-N Selection for LLMs via Self-Certainty
finding: Self-certainty (KL divergence of the next-token distribution from uniform, averaged over a response) separates correct and incorrect responses better than perplexity and is insensitive to response length. Borda-style weighted voting on it beats plain self-consistency. The paper says self-consistency is not applicable to open-ended outputs such as code (no shared answer string), while self-certainty applies and beat greedy decoding and universal self-consistency there.
numbers: Models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B (LiveCodeBench), one DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B run on MATH Level 3. Benchmarks: LiveBench-Math, GSM8K, MATH, CRUXEval, LiveCodeBench.
limits: Needs full logits. Small open models. One trial for the reasoning-model run.
agent_relevance: Code detail for gap 1: exact-match agreement does not exist for code. Agreement must be defined by behaviour (tests, outputs on probe inputs). That design step is hidden in the phrase k samples agree.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Coverage (some sample is right) keeps rising with samples, but picking the answer by majority vote or reward model plateaus. So agreement alone cannot find a minority-correct answer. Where an automatic verifier exists (unit tests, proof checker) coverage turns into accuracy.
numbers: MATH with Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000; majority vote or reward model only 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range. SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250, above the 43% single-sample state of the art.
limits: Small open models, 2024. Shows the plateau, not the rate of confidently wrong consensus.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 cheap check for code: run tests. Tests break false consensus because they do not vote. For non-code tasks the voting plateau means a second independent check (different framing, tool) is needed to rescue minority-correct answers.

source: Lin, Hilton, Evans (2022) TruthfulQA: measuring how models mimic human falsehoods
finding: Imitative falsehoods are wrong answers that appear often in training text, so a model gives them consistently. The largest models were generally the least truthful. This is the LLM version of the consensually wrong item.
numbers: 817 questions, 38 categories; best model truthful on 58% of questions, humans 94% (GPT-3, GPT-Neo/J, GPT-2, T5-based).
limits: 2021 models; newer models do much better on this set. Shows the class exists, not its current rate.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 partial: confirms the failure class exists in LLMs. How often it hits current frontier models on open-ended and code tasks was not found; that part stays open.

source: Spiess et al. (2024) Calibration and Correctness of Language Models for Code
finding: Code models are not well calibrated out of the box. Platt scaling helps but needs labelled data: more than 64 data points before skill turns positive, with gains continuing into the hundreds. A map fitted on one task transfers only to tasks of the same kind with similar base rates. Reflection-based confidence is inconsistent unless prompted with similar solved examples (BM25-selected few-shot raised skill from 0 to up to 0.15).
numbers: Example: line completions with average token probability above 90% passed tests only 52% of the time. Rescaling GPT-3.5 pNB between two function-synthesis tasks: skill score 0.14 -> 0.12, ECE 0.07 -> 0.05. Rescaling fitted on DyPyBench applied to function synthesis: skill score 0.12 -> -1.28, ECE 0.08 -> 0.54.
limits: Token and reflective confidence, not sample agreement. GPT-3.5, Codex, CodeGen2; several datasets per task.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: transfer is conditional. Fit one map per task family, check base-rate match, and expect to need a few hundred labelled items per family. Do not assume one held-out map covers code repair and code synthesis alike.

source: Dai and Wang (2026) Beyond 0-100: how confidence scale design shapes verbalized confidence and LLM metacognition
finding: Full text read. Six models: GPT-5.2, Gemini 3.1 Pro, LLaMA-4-Maverick, LLaMA-4-Scout, Qwen3-235B-A22B, Qwen3-30B-A3B (plus a dense Llama-3-8B for a robustness check). Verbalized confidence on 0-100 is heavily discretised. M-ratio (meta-d/d, from a single binarised threshold) at 0-100 runs from 0.62 (Qwen3-30B) to 0.92 (GPT-5.2). A 0-20 scale raised it for most models (GPT-5.2 0.95 vs 0.92; LLaMA-4-Maverick 0.89 vs 0.82). Raising the lower bound of the scale lowered it (GPT-5.2 0.92 down to 0.69 at the harshest shift; Qwen3-30B 0.62 down to 0.43).
numbers: Three most common values cover 78.2% to 92.1% of answers per model; models use only 15 to 28 of 101 values. Gemini 3.1 Pro says 100 on 68.4% of items but is right on only 79% of them; GPT-5.2 says 95 on 42.1% and is right on 85%. Entropy 0.95 to 1.88 bits. GPT-5.2 row (parsed from a garbled table): accuracy 0.81, AUROC 0.88, ECE 0.08, meta-d 1.84. Datasets MMLU (1,000), GSM8K (1,319), TruthfulQA (817). Temperature 0, N at least 800 per cell.
limits: v4 posted Oct 2026; preprint, not peer reviewed. Verbalized, single answer, greedy; not sample agreement. Binary meta-d from one threshold is cruder than the full type-2 ROC fit. The paper says AUROC stays high despite discretisation. Multiple-choice and short tasks.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 9 (original numbers confirm 0.62-0.92). Also a recent frontier data point for gap 8: verbalized efficiency is high at the top (0.92), but the scale itself moves the score, so a metric on a coarse verbal scale partly measures the prompt. A reason to prefer agreement-based confidence, which has a natural fine scale 0..k.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Six reasoning models against their non-reasoning twins, six datasets, verbalized confidence: reasoning models were strictly better calibrated in 33 of 36 settings. The gain comes from slow-thinking behaviour (trying alternatives, backtracking) and grows as the chain of thought unfolds; non-reasoning models improve when guided to slow-think in context. Qwen3 shows a large gap between thinking and non-thinking modes from one checkpoint.
numbers: Example: GLM-Z1 had 0.07 lower accuracy than GLM-4 on NonambigQA yet 0.037 lower ECE and 0.078 higher AUROC. Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct used the 85% or 95% bin for more than 80% of samples. Two-bin use inflated AUROC for non-reasoning models on multiple-choice sets (MMLU-Pro, SuperGPQA). Models are 32B open reasoning models (R1-Distill, QwQ, OR1, GLM-Z1, EXAONE-Deep, Qwen3).
limits: Greedy decoding mainly (sampling checked as a robustness test). Verbalized only; no agreement arm at equal tokens. 32B scale, not frontier API models.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 8: reasoning models are better at verbalized confidence, which narrows the case for agreement over verbalized for current models. Nobody here measured the two head to head at equal tokens, so gap 1 stays open. Also shows AUROC2 can be inflated by two-bin confidence: use many-level scores.

source: Mei et al. (2025) Reasoning about Uncertainty: Do Reasoning Models Know When They Don't Know?
finding: Verbalized confidence of API reasoning models (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek R1, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, o3-Mini) is typically overconfident, often above 85% even when wrong, especially on hard sets like SimpleQA. More reasoning effort made them more overconfident on wrongly answered questions. A second pass asking the model to reflect on its own trace (introspective UQ) improved o3-Mini and R1 but made Claude 3.7 worse.
numbers: Five benchmarks including a subset of ARC, GPQA and SimpleQA; metrics ECE and MCE. No table values copied; only the statements in the abstract and text.
limits: Verbalized confidence only; no sample-agreement arm. Early-2025 reasoning models. Abstract, introduction and setup read closely; result tables not.
agent_relevance: Contested with d16: reasoning models improve verbalized calibration in 32B open models but are overconfident in API reasoning models at higher effort. Another reason to measure agreement-based confidence directly instead of assuming the verbal one is fixed.

source: Kim, Liao, Vorvoreanu, Ballard, Vaughan (2024) 'I'm Not Sure, But...': uncertainty expression, user reliance and trust (FAccT 2024)
finding: Pre-registered experiment, N=404 after excluding 252 of 656 (38.4%). Medical yes/no questions; a fictional LLM search engine was correct on half the questions and expressed uncertainty on half, with the sets randomised. First-person hedges ('I'm not sure, but...') reduced agreement with the system and raised accuracy. General-perspective hedges had weaker, non-significant effects.
numbers: Accuracy: control 63.9%, first-person 72.8%, general 67.9% (n.s.), no-AI 74.2%. Agreement: control 80.9%, first-person 74.8%, general 77.6%, no-AI 58.4%. Control accuracy was 88.5% when the AI was right and 33.0% when it was wrong. Within the hedge conditions, accuracy on wrong-AI questions was 43.6% -> 52.0% (first-person) and 32.8% -> 48.0% (general) for non-hedged -> hedged answers; on right-AI questions it dipped (92.2 -> 89.2; 94.8 -> 83.1).
limits: The hedge was assigned by the experimenters, not computed from sample agreement or logprobs, so it tests wording and not signal quality. Control still trailed the no-AI baseline (63.9 vs 74.2): the AI hurt on average. Medical yes/no, MTurk.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 partial: wording alone moves human reliance and accuracy, and first-person phrasing works best. Whether a hedge truly tied to agreement helps more was not tested. Plan: render agreement k/n in first-person wording and test on a small human panel.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What large language models know and what people think they know (Nature Machine Intelligence)
finding: Detail added for gap 10. With default explanations people overestimated accuracy (calibration gap) and discriminated right from wrong barely above chance. Aligning the wording of the explanation with the model's token-based confidence narrowed both gaps. Longer explanations raised confidence without raising discrimination.
numbers: Model AUC 0.751 / 0.746 / 0.781 vs human AUC 0.589 / 0.602 / 0.592 (default). With long or uncertainty-only explanations human AUC 0.54 and 0.57 (BF = .23). Model ECE 0.104 and 0.154 vs human 0.291 (default) and 0.225 (modified) in panels read from a figure. Experiments 1a-2c had 41, 39, 42, 60, 60, 59 participants (301 in total, 284 retained).
limits: Wording matched to token likelihood, not to sample agreement. The pairing of ECE values to panels was read from a figure, so treat it as approximate.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: matched wording helps readers, and the effect sits in the explanation the reader sees. Agreement-derived confidence has not been tested with readers; transfer is plausible but unproven. Keep explanations short.

source: Cacioli (2026) metacognitive efficiency of LLM token confidence: limitations section
finding: The limitations section says generalisation to frontier scale is unknown, models ran as quantised 7-9B open weights, and API models without logprobs cannot be evaluated with this measure (the author points to Dai's verbal approach). After the scorer fix, 18.4% of answers the scorer still rejects are actually correct (630 blinded adjudications over seven models), and this residual rate varies 2.4-fold between models.
numbers: Residual scorer error 18.4%, model-dependent by a factor of 2.4. Four 8-9B models in the main study.
limits: Single author, not peer reviewed, three versions with a retraction of an earlier claim. Measures token log-probability confidence with meta-I2r.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open for large reasoning models: the paper says so itself. Treat any model ranking built on an automatic open-ended scorer as provisional until the scorer's residual error is below the gaps being measured.
